transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, um… the main thing is work, honestly. I’m a nurse, and when I’m on the floor I keep losing my train of thought. Like I’ll be trying to sort out a patient flow issue, and then an IV pump starts beeping, or someone asks another nurse a question near me, or a call light goes off, and it’s like—whatever I was just doing is gone.

And I know hospitals are noisy, that’s normal, but this feels… excessive. I’ll be standing there thinking, “Wait, what was I in the middle of?” It’s been really frustrating.
Do you find yourself getting distracted or losing your train of thought easily in other situations, like when you’re at home or talking with friends, or is this something that only happens at work?

I mean, work is definitely where I notice it the most, because the floor is just… constant. Like I’ll be right in the middle of figuring out a patient flow thing, and then an IV pump starts beeping, or someone nearby asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and suddenly it’s just gone. I’ll literally be standing there like, what was I doing?

I’m sure it happens other places too, but the main reason I’m here is that at work it’s constant and it’s really messing with me.

Can you think of a time when you were at home or in a quieter environment — maybe watching TV, reading, or talking with someone — and you suddenly lost your train of thought the same way you described at work?

Yeah, I mean… I’m trying to think of a specific home example, but honestly my mind keeps going back to the floor because that’s where it’s really obvious. Like I’ll be working through a patient flow issue, trying to figure out who needs what next, and then an IV pump beeps or a call light goes off, or someone near me asks another nurse something, and it’s like someone wiped the board clean. I just completely lose what I was doing.

At home, I guess it probably happens, but it doesn’t feel as urgent, you know? At work it’s constant, and it really throws me off because I can’t just pause everything and retrace my steps.
When you're at home watching TV or reading, do you find it hard to focus or stay engaged, or do you usually feel able to follow along without losing track?

I mean… with TV or reading, it’s harder for me to pin down because if I lose the thread, I can just rewind or reread a paragraph, and it doesn’t feel as dramatic.

But the main thing—the reason I’m here—is on the floor. I’ll be in the middle of a patient flow issue, like figuring out what needs to happen next, and then an IV pump beeps, or someone asks another nurse something nearby, or a call light goes off, and suddenly I’ve completely lost what I was working on. Like it just disappears. That’s the part that’s happening constantly and really messing me up.

When you’re at home doing something quiet and low-pressure, like watching TV, reading, or talking with a friend, do you ever find yourself losing focus or getting distracted easily, even if it’s not as intense as at work?

Yeah, I mean, sometimes, probably… like if I’m watching something and my phone buzzes or there’s noise outside, I’ll kind of drift and then realize I missed whatever just happened. But it’s hard for me to separate that from normal stuff, because at home I can just rewind it or ask, “Wait, what did you say?”

The thing that keeps sticking in my head is work, because there I can’t just rewind. I’ll be on the floor trying to sort out some patient flow thing—like who needs to go where or what needs to happen next—and then an IV pump beeps, or a call light goes off, or someone asks another nurse a question nearby, and it’s just… gone. I completely lose the thread of what I was doing. That’s the part that feels constant and really stressful.
Can you recall any instances in the past, such as during school or other jobs, where you had trouble keeping your focus, especially when tasks required sustained attention?

Yeah… school, definitely. I mean, it’s funny because I always think of this as a work problem now, but if I go back, even in elementary school my teachers would write stuff like, “She’s bright, but careless,” which—ugh, I hated that word. Or they’d say I wasn’t turning things in.

And it wasn’t always that I hadn’t done it. I’d lose the worksheet, or it would be shoved in my desk or my backpack, or I’d forget to hand in the homework even if my mom had watched me do it the night before. She used to have to sit with me every night to keep me on track, because otherwise I’d just… drift off or get stuck halfway through.

Sorry, I’m kind of going off, but yeah, it goes way back.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, even outside of work?

I… don’t know that I’d say hopeless. I mean, work has been stressing me out a lot, so sometimes I come home pretty wiped and I don’t feel like doing much, but I’m not sure if that’s the same thing.

Like, I still enjoy things when I actually get myself there—seeing a friend, watching something, going for a walk or whatever. Although then I’ll get distracted thinking about laundry or some random thing I forgot to buy, and then I’m in the kitchen opening cabinets for no reason… sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

But no, I haven’t really noticed feeling down all the time or losing interest in everything. It feels more like I’m overwhelmed than depressed, if that makes sense.

Outside of work and school, do you also notice these kinds of attention problems in your day-to-day life at home — like losing things, forgetting tasks, or getting easily sidetracked while doing routine activities?

Yes, definitely. At home it shows up a lot, honestly. I’ll forget things that should be basic, like calling my sister back or paying a bill, even though I fully meant to do it.

And I do the thing where I set a reminder, but then the reminder goes off while I’m in the middle of something else, and I’ll think, “Okay, I’ll do it in five minutes,” and then it’s just gone. Or I’ll miss an appointment because I had it in my head and then somehow didn’t connect it to the actual day.

It’s embarrassing because it’s not like I don’t care. I really do mean to follow through. I just get sidetracked so easily, and then later I’m like, wait, how did I forget that?
Do you often feel restless, fidgety, or as though you're constantly 'on the go' even when you're trying to relax or stay still?

Um… I’m not sure, actually. I don’t think of myself as “on the go” in that way? Like, I’m tired a lot of the time when I’m trying to relax, so I’ll sit down and then—well, sometimes I’m mentally jumping around, but physically restless… I don’t know.

I might tap my foot or mess with my hands if I’m waiting somewhere, but I’m not sure if that’s more than normal. My coworkers joke that I always have a pen in my hand, but nurses kind of do that anyway, so… yeah, I don’t know if I’d call it constant.
Have you ever found yourself acting without thinking, like interrupting others, blurting out answers, or feeling like you can't wait your turn?

I’m not really sure. I don’t think I’m the kind of person who’s always blurting things out or cutting people off, at least not that I notice.

Sometimes in conversation I’ll jump in because I’m worried I’ll forget what I was going to say, but then I’ll realize I maybe interrupted, and I feel bad. But I don’t know if that’s, like, an impulse thing or just normal conversation.

Waiting my turn… I mean, I don’t love waiting in lines, but who does? Actually, the grocery store line near my apartment is always weirdly slow because they only staff one lane, and then I start looking at all the random little snacks by the register and remember I forgot toothpaste—sorry. Um, no, I guess I haven’t really thought of myself as acting without thinking in that way.
Have you been feeling unusually tired or low on energy, even when you haven’t been doing anything particularly taxing?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I get tired, but I also work weird shifts sometimes, so it’s hard to tell what’s “unusual” versus just… life, you know?

Like, after a long day I’ll feel wiped out, but I don’t know that it happens when I haven’t done anything taxing. And then sometimes I’ll be sitting on the couch and feel drained, but I’ll realize I haven’t eaten properly or I stayed up scrolling—sorry, that’s probably not what you asked.

I guess I haven’t specifically noticed low energy out of nowhere.
Have you been feeling guilty or blaming yourself for things more than usual, even when it doesn’t seem entirely fair?

I’m not sure. I mean, I feel guilty about little things sometimes, like if I forgot to call someone back or I left laundry in the washer too long and then it smells weird—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

I don’t think I’ve been blaming myself more than usual, though. At work I’ll replay conversations in my head sometimes, but I think a lot of nurses do that because you’re always trying not to miss anything. So… I guess I haven’t noticed guilt being a big thing or anything that feels unfair.
Have you noticed yourself getting more irritable or frustrated than usual, even over small things, either at work or at home?

I don’t know… I mean, I get annoyed, sure, especially at work when things are busy or someone leaves supplies in the wrong place and then you’re hunting for flushes or tape or whatever. But I don’t think I’ve noticed being more irritable than usual.

At home, little things can bug me, like dishes in the sink, but then I’ll remember I also left half of them there, so it’s not exactly fair for me to get mad. And sometimes I’m just hungry or I haven’t had coffee, which makes everything feel more irritating than it probably is.

So… I guess no, not in a way that stands out to me.
Have you ever had periods where your mood felt unusually elevated, irritable, or energized for no clear reason, even if it didn’t last very long?

Um… I don’t think so? I mean, I have days where I get kind of wired, but usually there’s a reason, like too much coffee or a busy shift where you just don’t sit down for twelve hours and then somehow your body doesn’t know how to stop. And then I’ll come home and start cleaning random things, like the top of the fridge, which I never notice normally—sorry, that’s probably not what you mean.

Unusually elevated… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say I’ve had periods like that for no clear reason. Irritable, maybe if I’m stressed or tired, but not like out of nowhere that I’ve really noticed.
Do you often struggle to get started on tasks, keep things organized, or follow through to finish something once you’ve begun?

Yeah… yes. Especially the organizing and follow-through part. Like when I’m charge nurse, I’ll think I’m being organized because I have scraps of paper and sticky notes and half-started lists all over the place, but then it’s like I can’t figure out what actually needs to happen first.

So I end up just reacting to whatever is loudest or most urgent in the moment, and then by the end of the shift I’m rushing around trying to finish everything I meant to do earlier. And then I’ll find some note I wrote to myself like three hours ago and be like, oh, right, that was important.
Can you recall if these attention and organizational difficulties were present when you were a child, before the age of 12?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, my mom would probably have a whole file on this if you asked her.

In elementary school my teachers always wrote stuff like I was bright but careless, or that I needed to slow down, and I was constantly losing worksheets. Like they’d be in my backpack somewhere, or shoved in a folder with old permission slips and snack wrappers—my backpack was always this disaster zone.

And homework was a big thing. I’d do it sometimes and then just… not turn it in, which sounds ridiculous, but I really would forget. My mom had to sit with me pretty much every night to keep me on track, otherwise I’d drift off or get stuck sharpening pencils or reorganizing erasers or something. So yes, it was definitely there when I was a kid.
Have you ever found yourself feeling physically restless or fidgety to the point that it was difficult to sit still for extended periods, such as during meetings, meals, or travel?

I’m not sure… I mean, I don’t think of myself as someone who can’t sit still, exactly. Like, I can sit through a meal or a meeting if I have to, but I probably do mess with things—my pen, my badge reel, whatever’s in front of me.

Travel is weird because I get annoyed being stuck, but I don’t know if that’s restlessness or just… everyone hates airports, right? I once spent like forty minutes walking around a terminal because my gate changed and then I got distracted by one of those little stores that sells neck pillows and weirdly expensive trail mix—sorry, that’s not really the question.

So… I guess some fidgeting, maybe, but I’m not sure it’s to the point where I couldn’t sit still for long periods.
Have your attention difficulties ever caused problems in your personal relationships or led to any negative consequences at work, like errors or reprimands, despite your best efforts to manage them?

Yeah… unfortunately, yes. Work is the big one. I mean, I try so hard to compensate—I have lists, reminders, I’ll rewrite things in different colors, which sounds like I’m in middle school with gel pens, but it helps for maybe five minutes.

But it’s gotten serious enough that I’m on formal supervision now. And when I’m charge nurse, other nurses have to double-check parts of my follow-through, like making sure I didn’t miss something that I was supposed to circle back to. Which is… honestly really embarrassing.

Because I’m supposed to be the person leading and keeping everything moving, and instead I feel like people are watching me because they’re worried I’ll drop something. It makes me feel like I’m becoming a liability instead of a leader, even though I’m really trying.

Um… I’m not sure, actually. I don’t think of myself as “on the go” in that way? Like, I’m tired a lot of the time when I’m trying to relax, so I’ll sit down and then—well, sometimes I’m mentally jumping around, but physically restless… I don’t know.

I might tap my foot or mess with my hands if I’m waiting somewhere, but I’m not sure if that’s more than normal. My coworkers joke that I always have a pen in my hand, but nurses kind of do that anyway, so… yeah, I don’t know if I’d call it constant.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of hyperactivity or impulsivity that may support a diagnosis of ADHD (F48.0).
doctor.question: Have you ever found yourself acting without thinking, like interrupting others, blurting out answers, or feeling like you can't wait your turn?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about impulsivity symptoms such as interrupting, blurting out, or difficulty waiting turns, which are not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. I don’t think I’m the kind of person who’s always blurting things out or cutting people off, at least not that I notice.

Sometimes in conversation I’ll jump in because I’m worried I’ll forget what I was going to say, but then I’ll realize I maybe interrupted, and I feel bad. But I don’t know if that’s, like, an impulse thing or just normal conversation.

Waiting my turn… I mean, I don’t love waiting in lines, but who does? Actually, the grocery store line near my apartment is always weirdly slow because they only staff one lane, and then I start looking at all the random little snacks by the register and remember I forgot toothpaste—sorry. Um, no, I guess I haven’t really thought of myself as acting without thinking in that way.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of fatigue or low energy that could support a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F32.9).
doctor.question: Have you been feeling unusually tired or low on energy, even when you haven’t been doing anything particularly taxing?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about fatigue or low energy, which is not covered by the provided ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. I mean, I get tired, but I also work weird shifts sometimes, so it’s hard to tell what’s “unusual” versus just… life, you know?

Like, after a long day I’ll feel wiped out, but I don’t know that it happens when I haven’t done anything taxing. And then sometimes I’ll be sitting on the couch and feel drained, but I’ll realize I haven’t eaten properly or I stayed up scrolling—sorry, that’s probably not what you asked.

I guess I haven’t specifically noticed low energy out of nowhere.

doctor.intent: Assess presence of symptoms of depression, specifically feelings of worthlessness or guilt, which would support a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F32.9).
doctor.question: Have you been feeling guilty or blaming yourself for things more than usual, even when it doesn’t seem entirely fair?

target_item.reason: The question is about excessive or inappropriate guilt/self-blame, which is more related to mood/depressive symptoms and is not covered by the listed ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. I mean, I feel guilty about little things sometimes, like if I forgot to call someone back or I left laundry in the washer too long and then it smells weird—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

I don’t think I’ve been blaming myself more than usual, though. At work I’ll replay conversations in my head sometimes, but I think a lot of nurses do that because you’re always trying not to miss anything. So… I guess I haven’t noticed guilt being a big thing or anything that feels unfair.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of emotional dysregulation or irritability, which are relevant to differentiating between ADHD and other conditions like adjustment disorder or depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself getting more irritable or frustrated than usual, even over small things, either at work or at home?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about irritability or frustration, which is not covered by the provided ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… I mean, I get annoyed, sure, especially at work when things are busy or someone leaves supplies in the wrong place and then you’re hunting for flushes or tape or whatever. But I don’t think I’ve noticed being more irritable than usual.

At home, little things can bug me, like dishes in the sink, but then I’ll remember I also left half of them there, so it’s not exactly fair for me to get mad. And sometimes I’m just hungry or I haven’t had coffee, which makes everything feel more irritating than it probably is.

So… I guess no, not in a way that stands out to me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of emotional dysregulation or mood instability that could indicate a mood disorder such as bipolar disorder (F32.9 could be major depressive episode, but differential with F06.81 which can include mood symptoms due to another medical condition)
doctor.question: Have you ever had periods where your mood felt unusually elevated, irritable, or energized for no clear reason, even if it didn’t last very long?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about possible manic or hypomanic episodes—unusually elevated, irritable, or energized mood—which is not covered by the provided ADHD inattentive symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Um… I don’t think so? I mean, I have days where I get kind of wired, but usually there’s a reason, like too much coffee or a busy shift where you just don’t sit down for twelve hours and then somehow your body doesn’t know how to stop. And then I’ll come home and start cleaning random things, like the top of the fridge, which I never notice normally—sorry, that’s probably not what you mean.

Unusually elevated… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say I’ve had periods like that for no clear reason. Irritable, maybe if I’m stressed or tired, but not like out of nowhere that I’ve really noticed.

doctor.intent: Assessing for the presence of symptoms of executive dysfunction in ADHD, specifically difficulty with task initiation, organization, and follow-through, which could differentiate F48.0 (ADHD) from other conditions.
doctor.question: Do you often struggle to get started on tasks, keep things organized, or follow through to finish something once you’ve begun?

target_item.name: Organization_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: When I’m charge nurse, I have scraps of paper, sticky notes, and half-started lists everywhere, but I still can’t seem to decide what has to happen first, so I end up putting out whatever fire is loudest and then rushing at the end of the shift.
target_item.reason: The question most directly asks about struggling to keep tasks organized and manage follow-through, which matches difficulty organizing tasks and activities.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes. Especially the organizing and follow-through part. Like when I’m charge nurse, I’ll think I’m being organized because I have scraps of paper and sticky notes and half-started lists all over the place, but then it’s like I can’t figure out what actually needs to happen first.

So I end up just reacting to whatever is loudest or most urgent in the moment, and then by the end of the shift I’m rushing around trying to finish everything I meant to do earlier. And then I’ll find some note I wrote to myself like three hours ago and be like, oh, right, that was important.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms are present in childhood, which is key for diagnosing ADHD (F48.0).
doctor.question: Can you recall if these attention and organizational difficulties were present when you were a child, before the age of 12?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even in elementary school, my teachers wrote that I was bright but careless and always losing worksheets or forgetting to turn in homework, and my mom had to sit with me every night to keep me on track.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether the attention and organizational difficulties were present in childhood before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I mean, my mom would probably have a whole file on this if you asked her.

In elementary school my teachers always wrote stuff like I was bright but careless, or that I needed to slow down, and I was constantly losing worksheets. Like they’d be in my backpack somewhere, or shoved in a folder with old permission slips and snack wrappers—my backpack was always this disaster zone.

And homework was a big thing. I’d do it sometimes and then just… not turn it in, which sounds ridiculous, but I really would forget. My mom had to sit with me pretty much every night to keep me on track, otherwise I’d drift off or get stuck sharpening pencils or reorganizing erasers or something. So yes, it was definitely there when I was a kid.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of hyperactivity or restlessness that are impairing, which would support a diagnosis of ADHD (F48.0).
doctor.question: Have you ever found yourself feeling physically restless or fidgety to the point that it was difficult to sit still for extended periods, such as during meetings, meals, or travel?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about physical restlessness or fidgetiness and difficulty sitting still, but the provided symptom profile does not include that symptom.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure… I mean, I don’t think of myself as someone who can’t sit still, exactly. Like, I can sit through a meal or a meeting if I have to, but I probably do mess with things—my pen, my badge reel, whatever’s in front of me.

Travel is weird because I get annoyed being stuck, but I don’t know if that’s restlessness or just… everyone hates airports, right? I once spent like forty minutes walking around a terminal because my gate changed and then I got distracted by one of those little stores that sells neck pillows and weirdly expensive trail mix—sorry, that’s not really the question.

So… I guess some fidgeting, maybe, but I’m not sure it’s to the point where I couldn’t sit still for long periods.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant impairment in social or occupational functioning due to attention symptoms, beyond what would be expected in a typical high-pressure job like nursing.
doctor.question: Have your attention difficulties ever caused problems in your personal relationships or led to any negative consequences at work, like errors or reprimands, despite your best efforts to manage them?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work, the concerns have gotten serious enough that I’m on formal supervision and other nurses have to double-check parts of my charge-nurse follow-through, which makes me feel like I’m becoming a liability instead of a leader.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the attention difficulties have caused real-life consequences in relationships or at work, such as errors or reprimands, which is most directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah… unfortunately, yes. Work is the big one. I mean, I try so hard to compensate—I have lists, reminders, I’ll rewrite things in different colors, which sounds like I’m in middle school with gel pens, but it helps for maybe five minutes.

But it’s gotten serious enough that I’m on formal supervision now. And when I’m charge nurse, other nurses have to double-check parts of my follow-through, like making sure I didn’t miss something that I was supposed to circle back to. Which is… honestly really embarrassing.

Because I’m supposed to be the person leading and keeping everything moving, and instead I feel like people are watching me because they’re worried I’ll drop something. It makes me feel like I’m becoming a liability instead of a leader, even though I’m really trying.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms of inattention, distractibility, and organizational difficulties have been present since childhood and persist into adulthood, significantly impacting her work as a nurse and leading to formal supervision. These symptoms are not better explained by other disorders such as mood or psychotic disorders (F32.9, F06.81), and there is no evidence of chronic stress-related disorders (F43.22). The clinical picture is consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation, coded as F48.0 (F48.00 in some systems, but F48.0 is the general code for ADHD in ICD-10).

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent inattention, distractibility, and difficulties with organization and task completion, dating back to childhood and persisting into adulthood. These symptoms are consistent with Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), predominantly inattentive presentation.
